Before Shoushan was Nan’uan Yong; however, the "Daxian" edition is fundamentally erroneous.
Furthermore, the sequence of the "Daxian" edition is inverted. Now, relying on the Gushan edition, I have compiled this catalog to correct it.

Regarding its catalog: the *Xinhuabentianji* (Collection of the Original Heaven of the Mind’s Flower) was originally placed at the beginning [of the manuscript], but following the *Zahua* (Miscellaneous Flower) edition, it has now been moved to the beginning of the *Zhengji* (Correct Collection).
The *Daxianben* (Original Text of the Great Immortal), comprising eighty-three *zhang* from Yexian, Shimen, and Zhaozhou, has been added to the *Tianji*.
Furthermore, the titles and wrappers have been prepared for the one hundred and nineteen *zhang* comprising Shoushan, Shending, Linji, Chengtian, Nanquan, Tiantong, Muzhou, and others.
It is the *Diji* (Earth Collection). This is the original source of the *Daxian* (Great Sage) collection; it has fundamentally lost the *Diji*.

Furthermore, eight sections were missing from the *Tianji* (Heaven Collection), so I have used the Gushan edition to compile the first and second fascicles, merely filling in the omissions in the *Tianji* and *Diji*.
It can be seen that even the titles of the folded pages differ from those of the *Tianji*, *Riji* (Day Collection), and others.
The Xiangguo edition: from Fayen Yi to Jingu Shizhi, comprising sixteen houses, constitutes the *Diji* (Collection on the Ground).
The Daxian edition is entirely missing.
The Daxian edition: from Nanquan Yuan to Shimen Cong, totaling nine houses; the Xiangguo edition is complete.
They were not included. All nine cases are found in the currently published *Records of Ancient Worthies* (*Gu zunsu lu*).

Since they were originally compiled by [the author of] the Gushan edition, they do not constitute a "Continued Record" (*Xulu*); therefore, they cannot be added to the *Continued Records of Ancient Worthies*.

The Shinne-in of Sōgō-ji formerly housed the *Xù gǔ zūnshǒu lù* (Continued Record of Ancient Venerable Masters).
I once visited Master Fángzhǔ at Dàguānmíng-sì and was able to examine it. After Zhǔ passed away, his successor also died.
I mentioned this matter to Master Bóyīng of Xīngshèng-sì in Northern Jīng, and Yīng said, "I once borrowed it from Fángzhǔ and have made a copy."

I have long cherished this as a rare treasure. I was delighted to request its transcription; however, the original lacked the two collections on the *nakṣatras* (stellar mansions). I suspected that these had been neglected or lost.

In the winter of the seventh year of the Hyōhō era (1722), the year of Renyin, the former head of Zappō-in, Besson, acquired an ancient printed edition of the *Gozusokuroku* (Records of Ancient Venerable Masters) from the *Zhengxù* (Continued Collection) and showed it to me.
Each volume of this manuscript bore the seal of the Xīnhuá (Heart Flower) collection.

I felt deeply saddened by this. Since the second and third volumes on the constellations (*xingchen*) were missing from the *Xùlù* (Continued Record), I realized that these had not been transcribed by Yǎng;

they were simply omitted from the original manuscript, rather than being lost due to negligence. I recently borrowed a copy from Dàxiān Temple in Nóngzhōu. Bényuán further lent me another to transcribe the two volumes on the constellations.
I have also relied upon the Xīnhuā manuscript to complete and supplement the *Dàxiān běndì quánjì* (Complete Collection of the Original Grounds of Dàxiān Temple).

Regarding the "Half-Collection of the Celestial Assembly" (Tianji banzhi yi), I also maintain that although its primary records were all included in the *Ancient Records of Venerable Patriarchs* (*Guzunsu lu*) within the Northern Canon, they were originally compiled by [the monk] Gushan Ben.
This sufficiently reveals their original form. Consequently, I borrowed the *Zahua* edition and completed the transcription.
Thus, both the *Zahua* and *Longhua* editions have each obtained the ancient compilations of the *Continued Ancient Records of Venerable Patriarchs*.
How extraordinary! How exhilarating! Recorded by Daozhong.

The Master’s name was Yixuan. He was a native of Nanhua in Caizhou, with the secular surname Xing. From his youth he was exceptionally gifted, and as he grew up, he became renowned for his filial piety.
Upon shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he resided at lecture halls where he thoroughly investigated the *vinaya* and extensively contemplated the sutras and śāstras.
Suddenly, he sighed and said: "These are merely medical prescriptions for saving the world; they are not the ultimate purport of the separate transmission outside the teachings."

He immediately changed his robes and traveled to various regions. First he visited Huangbo, and next he called upon Dayu; the dialogues and exchanges between them are recorded in his *Xinglu* (Record of Conduct).
Having received the seal of approval from Huangbo, he soon arrived at the southeastern corner of the city of Zhenzhou in Hebei.
By the banks of the Hutuo River, there was a small monastery where Linji resided; it was there that he gained his name.

At that time, Puhua was already at that place, feigning madness and mingling with the common crowd, such that neither sages nor ordinary people could fathom him. When the Master arrived, he immediately assisted him.
As the Master’s influence flourished, Puhua cast off his physical body entirely, thereby fulfilling the prophetic prediction of Yangshan, who had called him the "Little Śākyamuni. It happened thus.

During the Ding era, when there was military conflict, the army abandoned the city and departed. Grand Marshal Mo Junhe donated his residence within the city to establish a temple, naming it after Linji, and invited the Master to dwell there.
Later, the Master shook out his robes and traveled south to Hedong Prefecture.
There, the Prefectural Governor, Attendant Wang, received him with the etiquette due to a teacher. After staying for only a short time, he proceeded to Xinghua Temple in Daming Prefecture.
He resided in the Eastern Hall. The Master was free from illness, yet one day he suddenly adjusted his robes, sat upright, and after concluding a dialogue with Sansheng, passed away in silence.
This was on the tenth day of the first month of the eighth year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, the Dinghai year.

The disciples enshrined the Master’s entire remains and erected a stupa at the northwest corner of Daming Fu. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Huizhao, and his stupa was named Chengling.
With palms joined and heads bowed, I record the Master’s principal deeds. He resided at Baoshou Monastery in Zhenzhou.
Written respectfully by the junior dharma-disciple Yanzhao.
